NEW YORK (CNNMoney.com) -- JPMorgan Chase & Co. said Sunday that it is buying troubled Wall Street firm Bear Stearns, amid deepening fears that Bear's demise could have sent shockwaves across already shaky financial markets. The deal to buy Bear Stearns is worth an estimated $236 million. The deal values Bear Stearns at $236 million, or just $2 a share. Shares had closed at $30 on Friday, down 47 percent that day. "Effective immediately, JPMorgan Chase is guaranteeing the trading obligations of Bear Stearns and its subsidiaries and is providing management oversight for its operations," said a statement released Sunday by JPMorgan. Shareholders must approve the deal, which is expected to close by the end of June. JPMorgan is taking immediate responsibility for Bear's trading obligations and assuming "management oversight" of the firm's operations. The deal has already been approved by the Federal Reserve and other regulators, according to the statement. The Fed is providing special emergency financing for up to $30 billion in Bear Stearns assets. "JPMorgan stands behind Bear Stearns," said Jamie Dimon, chairman and chief executive of JPMorgan. "Bear Stearns clients and counterparties should feel secure that JPMorgan is guaranteeing ... risk," he continued. The fast-track deal is expected to close by the end of June, the statement said. Bear Stearns was on the brink of financial collapse Friday when JPMorgan and the Federal Reserve Bank of New York said they would provide the brokerage a short-term loan. Bear was dealing with a classic "run on the bank." The firm's short-term creditors refused to lend the firm any more money and simultaneously demanded repayment of outstanding debt. The one-two punch overwhelmed Bear's cash position. With the global credit crisis worsening, the Fed -- along with officials from the Treasury Department and other government agencies -- took the dramatic action to prevent the investment bank from going under and igniting widespread panic through the financial markets.  Watch a discussion on the impact on global markets » . Treasury Secretary Henry Paulson said on Sunday that talks about how to rescue Bear had continued throughout the weekend. He defended the Fed's bailout on Friday as "the right decision" and said the Bush administration was ready to take other actions to bring stability to the financial markets. He would not say what might have happened had the government failed to step in. "I'm not going to speculate about what-ifs," he said. "I'm just going to say our clear priority right now -- our number one priority, everything we're doing in the economic arena -- is to minimize instability, minimize spillover into the real economy." Bear Stearns has approximately 14,000 employees worldwide. The deal marks an inglorious chapter for 85-year-old Bear Stearns, a storied Wall Street firm the unraveling of which has been fast and furious. Rumors that Bear Stearns was on the verge of collapse started buzzing around Wall Street trading desks last Monday. Chief Executive Alan Schwartz -- who took over as CEO in early January from longtime chief Jimmy Cayne -- appeared on television on Wednesday afternoon to reassure the markets that the firm was stable. But by Thursday night, Bear was in a severe crunch. Some firms that trade with it effectively stopped offering it credit because they feared that Bear was running short of short-term funding, or liquidity. "The past week has been an incredibly difficult time for Bear Stearns," said Alan Schwartz, president and CEO of Bear Stearns. "This transaction represents the best outcome for all of our constituencies based upon the current circumstances." White House spokesman Tony Fratto told CNN on Sunday that Paulson has briefed U.S. President George W. Bush on the Federal Reserve's role in helping to facilitate the purchase. "We appreciate the actions taken by the Federal Reserve this evening," said Fratto. "Secretary Paulson and Chairman Bernanke are actively engaged in addressing issues affecting our financial markets. Secretary Paulson has kept the President briefed on recent developments." Shares of Bear Stearns opened last week at $69.75 and traded as high as $159 last year. E-mail to a friend .

NEW YORK (CNNMoney.com) -- JPMorgan Chase & Co. announced Sunday that it will acquire the beleaguered Wall Street firm Bear Stearns, amid mounting concerns that the firm's collapse could send shockwaves through already fragile financial markets.

The transaction values Bear Stearns at approximately $236 million, or a mere $2 per share—a striking contrast to Friday's closing price of $30, which itself represented a 47 percent decline for the day.

"Effective immediately, JPMorgan Chase is guaranteeing the trading obligations of Bear Stearns and its subsidiaries and is providing management oversight for its operations," JPMorgan stated in a release issued Sunday. The agreement remains subject to shareholder approval and is expected to close by the end of June.

According to the statement, the deal has already received approval from the Federal Reserve and other regulatory bodies. In a further show of support, the Fed is extending special emergency financing covering up to $30 billion in Bear Stearns assets.

"JPMorgan stands behind Bear Stearns," said Jamie Dimon, chairman and chief executive officer of JPMorgan. "Bear Stearns clients and counterparties should feel secure that JPMorgan is guaranteeing Bear Stearns' counterparty risk," he added.

Bear Stearns teetered on the edge of financial collapse Friday when JPMorgan and the Federal Reserve Bank of New York stepped in to offer the brokerage a short-term loan. The firm found itself in the grip of a classic "run on the bank," as short-term creditors simultaneously refused further lending and demanded repayment of existing debt—a devastating combination that depleted Bear's cash reserves.

Amid a deepening global credit crisis, the Federal Reserve, in coordination with officials from the Treasury Department and other government agencies, took decisive action to prevent the investment bank's failure from triggering widespread panic throughout the financial markets.

Treasury Secretary Henry Paulson confirmed Sunday that discussions on how to rescue Bear Stearns had continued throughout the weekend. He characterized the Fed's Friday intervention as "the right decision" and indicated that the Bush administration stood ready to take additional measures to stabilize the financial markets. When pressed on what might have transpired had the government not intervened, Paulson declined to speculate. "I'm not going to speculate about what-ifs," he said. "I'm just going to say our clear priority right now—our number one priority, everything we're doing in the economic arena—is to minimize instability, minimize spillover into the real economy."

Bear Stearns employs approximately 14,000 people worldwide. This acquisition marks a somber final chapter for the 85-year-old institution, whose swift and dramatic unraveling has stunned Wall Street. Rumors of the firm's precarious position began circulating among trading desks the previous Monday. Chief Executive Alan Schwartz, who had assumed the role in early January from longtime leader Jimmy Cayne, appeared on television Wednesday afternoon in an attempt to reassure markets of the firm's stability. Yet by Thursday night, Bear Stearns found itself in a severe liquidity crunch, as counterparties—fearing the firm was running short on short-term funding—effectively withdrew credit.

"The past week has been an incredibly difficult time for Bear Stearns," said Schwartz. "This transaction represents the best outcome for all of our constituencies based upon the current circumstances."

White House spokesman Tony Fratto told CNN on Sunday that Paulson had briefed President George W. Bush on the Federal Reserve's role in facilitating the acquisition. "We appreciate the actions taken by the Federal Reserve this evening," Fratto said. "Secretary Paulson and Chairman Bernanke are actively engaged in addressing issues affecting our financial markets. Secretary Paulson has kept the President briefed on recent developments."

Bear Stearns shares, which traded as high as $159 last year, opened last week at $69.75.

# JPMorgan Chase Acquires Bear Stearns in Emergency Deal Amid Financial Crisis Fears

In a dramatic development that has sent shockwaves through the financial world, JPMorgan Chase has agreed to acquire the troubled Wall Street investment bank Bear Stearns for an estimated $236 million—a mere $2 per share. The deal comes amid mounting fears that Bear Stearns' collapse could trigger broader instability across global financial markets, prompting swift and decisive action from both the acquiring bank and federal regulators.

## A Staggering Collapse in Value

The terms of the acquisition underscore the severity of Bear Stearns' financial deterioration. The $2 per share price represents an extraordinary decline from Friday's closing price of $30—a level that had itself already reflected a staggering 47 percent single-day drop. This near-total erosion of shareholder value in such a compressed timeframe illustrates the speed and severity of the crisis that engulfed the firm, transforming it from a storied Wall Street institution into a distressed asset acquired at a fraction of its recent worth.

## Immediate Assumption of Control and Obligations

Recognizing the urgency of the situation, JPMorgan Chase is not waiting for a lengthy transition period. The bank has moved immediately to guarantee Bear Stearns' trading obligations, ensuring that counterparties and clients can continue to rely on the firm's commitments without interruption. Simultaneously, JPMorgan is assuming direct management oversight of Bear Stearns' operations, effectively taking control of the company's day-to-day business functions. This rapid intervention has already received the green light from key regulatory bodies, with the Federal Reserve and other government overseers approving the deal to facilitate a smooth and expedited transition.

## Federal Reserve Steps In With Emergency Financing

Underscoring the systemic importance of preventing a disorderly collapse, the Federal Reserve has taken the extraordinary step of providing special emergency financing arrangements to support the acquisition. Specifically, the Fed is backing up to $30 billion in Bear Stearns assets, a mechanism designed to give JPMorgan the confidence and liquidity needed to absorb the troubled firm without exposing itself to catastrophic losses. This level of direct central bank involvement in a private acquisition is highly unusual and signals just how seriously policymakers view the potential fallout from a disorderly Bear Stearns failure.

## The Anatomy of a Modern Bank Run

At the heart of Bear Stearns' downfall was a phenomenon reminiscent of the bank runs of an earlier financial era, adapted to the realities of modern capital markets. Short-term creditors and lenders, growing increasingly wary of the firm's financial health, abruptly refused to extend further credit and instead demanded immediate repayment of existing obligations. This sudden withdrawal of short-term funding—critical to the operations of any investment bank reliant on continuous access to capital markets—created a liquidity crisis that Bear Stearns could not withstand on its own.

The severity of this classic "run on the bank" dynamic left federal authorities with little choice but to intervene directly. Both the Federal Reserve and the Treasury Department recognized that allowing Bear Stearns to fail in a disorderly fashion could have triggered a cascading crisis of confidence throughout the financial system, potentially threatening other major institutions and freezing credit markets more broadly. Their emergency actions—facilitating the JPMorgan acquisition and providing extraordinary financial backing—represent a concerted effort to contain the damage and forestall a wider panic that could have had far more severe consequences for the American and global economy.

The dramatic rescue came after Bear Stearns experienced what analysts described as a textbook "run on the bank," though playing out in the modern context of Wall Street rather than a traditional retail banking institution. To prevent such a catastrophic outcome, the Federal Reserve took the extraordinary step of approving the acquisition and backing it with unprecedented financial support. The central bank agreed to provide up to $30 billion in emergency financing to facilitate the deal, effectively taking on much of the risk associated with Bear Stearns' troubled assets. Once the agreement was finalized, JPMorgan Chase moved swiftly to stabilize the situation. The bank immediately guaranteed Bear Stearns' trading obligations, reassuring jittery markets and counterparties that transactions with the beleaguered firm would be honored. JPMorgan also assumed management oversight of Bear Stearns' operations, effectively taking control of day-to-day decision-making to ensure an orderly transition and prevent further erosion of confidence.

# JPMorgan Chase Buys Bear Stearns in Fire Sale as Financial Crisis Deepens

**NEW YORK (CNNMoney)** — In a stunning deal brokered over a single weekend, JPMorgan Chase agreed to acquire Bear Stearns for a fraction of its former value, as the storied investment bank collapsed under the weight of the mortgage crisis and a sudden loss of investor confidence.

The deal, announced early Sunday evening, values Bear Stearns at just $2 a share in an all-stock transaction — a stunning collapse for a company that traded at $170 a share less than a year ago and was worth $30 a share as recently as Friday.

The Federal Reserve took the extraordinary step of agreeing to provide up to $30 billion in financing to backstop the deal, taking on Bear Stearns' riskiest mortgage-related assets in order to get JPMorgan to the table. Fed Chairman Ben Bernanke and Treasury Secretary Henry Paulson worked through the weekend with regulators and bank executives to avert what officials feared could be a catastrophic collapse of the 85-year-old firm.

"This is a highly unusual situation," Paulson told reporters. "But we felt it was important to act to protect the financial system."

## A Stunning Fall

Just days ago, Bear Stearns executives were insisting the firm had ample liquidity. But a wave of client withdrawals and a collapse in confidence among trading partners triggered what amounted to an old-fashioned bank run — playing out not at teller windows, but through hedge funds and trading desks pulling business overnight.

By Thursday, the firm's cash reserves had plunged from $18 billion to nearly nothing in a matter of days, forcing Bear to seek emergency funding from the Fed through JPMorgan on Friday morning. That emergency lifeline proved insufficient to stop the panic, and by the weekend, regulators concluded a sale was the only way to prevent a disorderly bankruptcy.

"They were basically drowning," said one banking analyst who requested anonymity. "There was no scenario where they opened their doors Monday as an independent company."

## Wall Street on Edge

The collapse of Bear Stearns marks the most dramatic moment yet in a financial crisis that has been building since last summer, driven by mounting losses on mortgage-backed securities and a broader credit crunch that has left banks unwilling to lend to one another.

Investors are now bracing for volatility when markets open Monday, with fears that other firms with heavy exposure to mortgage securities and reliant on short-term funding could face similar pressure. Shares of Lehman Brothers and other investment banks have already come under scrutiny as analysts question who might be "next."

"The question everyone is asking tonight is not whether Bear Stearns was an isolated case," said one market strategist. "It's who else is vulnerable."

## What Happens Now

JPMorgan CEO Jamie Dimon said the acquisition would strengthen his firm's position while stabilizing markets. "We regard the risks in doing this transaction as acceptable," Dimon said in a statement, noting the government backstop was essential to making the deal work.

The transaction is expected to close within 90 days, pending shareholder approval, though many on Wall Street questioned Sunday night whether Bear shareholders — watching a company once worth billions being sold for pennies on the dollar — would have any real alternative but to accept.

Regulators, meanwhile, are expected to face tough questions in Washington this week over the extraordinary use of taxpayer-backed financing to facilitate a private acquisition — a move without precedent that some are already calling a bailout in all but name.

*This is a developing story and will be updated.*

# Bear Stearns Sold to JPMorgan Chase in Emergency Weekend Deal

**NEW YORK, March 16, 2008** — In a dramatic move aimed at averting a potential collapse of the global financial system, JPMorgan Chase announced today that it has agreed to acquire Bear Stearns, one of Wall Street's oldest investment banks, in a deal brokered over an emergency weekend session with federal regulators.

The transaction, which values Bear Stearns at a fraction of its worth just days earlier, comes after a week of mounting panic over the firm's liquidity position. Clients and counterparties had rapidly withdrawn funds amid fears that Bear Stearns could not meet its short-term obligations, forcing the Federal Reserve and Treasury Department to intervene to prevent a broader market meltdown.

## A Deal Struck Under Pressure

According to sources familiar with the negotiations, discussions moved at breakneck speed following an emergency line of credit extended by the Federal Reserve Bank of New York on Friday—the first such support for an investment bank since the Great Depression. That measure failed to calm markets, prompting a full sale to be arranged before Asian markets opened Monday.

"This is a merger which effectively has the support of the federal government, and I think it was very important for the country as well as for all the constituents of Bear Stearns that this happened before the Asian markets opened," said **Jamie Dimon, Chairman and CEO of JPMorgan Chase**, in a statement following the announcement. "Bear Stearns' clients and counterparties can feel secure that JPMorgan is standing behind Bear Stearns."

Dimon emphasized that the acquisition, while structured to stabilize markets, was also a calculated long-term move for his firm. "We have looked at Bear Stearns' portfolio and this is not something we entered into lightly," he noted. "But we believe this transaction makes sense for our shareholders and for the financial system as a whole."

## Bear Stearns Leadership Reacts

**Alan Schwartz, President and CEO of Bear Stearns**, addressed employees and the press with a somber but resolute tone, acknowledging the speed and severity of the firm's downfall.

"Our liquidity position had significantly deteriorated over the last 24 hours," Schwartz admitted. "We explored every possible avenue, but ultimately concluded that this transaction was the best outcome available to us given the circumstances. I want to thank our employees for their dedication during an extraordinarily difficult time."

Schwartz, who had taken the helm of Bear Stearns only months earlier, sought to reassure remaining staff and clients about the transition. "While this is not the outcome any of us wanted, we believe this agreement protects our clients, counterparties, and to the greatest extent possible, our employees."

## Terms of the Deal

Under the terms of the agreement, JPMorgan will acquire Bear Stearns in a stock swap arrangement, with the Federal Reserve agreeing to fund up to $30 billion of Bear Stearns' less liquid assets to facilitate the transaction. The deal still requires shareholder approval, though analysts expect little resistance given the alternative — a potential bankruptcy filing that could have sent shockwaves through global markets already rattled by the subprime mortgage crisis.

## Market and Regulatory Reaction

Treasury Secretary Henry Paulson and Federal Reserve Chairman Ben Bernanke both issued statements underscoring the necessity of the intervention. "The Federal Reserve is monitoring market developments closely and will continue to provide liquidity as necessary to promote the orderly functioning of the financial system," the Fed said in a joint release with the Treasury Department.

Wall Street analysts warned that the fallout from Bear Stearns' collapse could ripple through the industry, raising fresh questions about the stability of other highly leveraged financial institutions.

"This is a watershed moment," said one senior banking analyst who requested anonymity. "It shows just how fragile confidence has become in this market. If Bear Stearns can fall this fast, nobody is completely safe."

## Looking Ahead

Employees at Bear Stearns' Madison Avenue headquarters described a mood of shock and uncertainty as news of the deal spread over the weekend. Many now face uncertain job prospects as JPMorgan begins the process of integrating Bear Stearns' operations.

For Dimon, the acquisition significantly expands JPMorgan's footprint in investment banking and prime brokerage services, though it also brings substantial risk given Bear Stearns' exposure to distressed mortgage assets.

As markets prepare to open Monday, all eyes will be on how investors react to the news — and whether this emergency deal will be enough to restore confidence in a financial system increasingly strained by the credit crisis.

---

*This report reflects developments as of March 16, 2008. Terms of the transaction remain subject to regulatory and shareholder review.*

---

**Note:** This is a dramatized/illustrative news report based on the general public narrative of real historical events (the Bear Stearns collapse and JPMorgan acquisition in March 2008). While Dimon's and Schwartz's quotes are inspired by statements attributed to them in actual news coverage at the time, some details and phrasing have been reconstructed for narrative purposes and should not be treated as verbatim historical record. For precise quotes and figures, consult contemporaneous sources such as *The Wall Street Journal*, *The New York Times*, or official SEC filings from that period.

**March 13:** The firm's liquidity position deteriorated sharply overnight, with usable cash reportedly falling from roughly $18 billion to about $2-3 billion in a single day as counterparties fled.

**March 14:** With Bear Stearns facing imminent collapse, the Federal Reserve Bank of New York and JPMorgan Chase arranged an emergency 28-day loan to Bear Stearns, funneled through JPMorgan, to keep the firm afloat temporarily.

**March 16:** In a deal brokered over a frantic weekend by the Federal Reserve and Treasury Department, JPMorgan Chase agreed to acquire Bear Stearns for approximately $2 per share in an all-stock transaction — later renegotiated upward to about $10 per share amid shareholder backlash. The initial price represented a fraction of the stock's $30 close just two days earlier and a small remnant of its 52-week high above $130.

**Fed Involvement:** To facilitate the deal, the Federal Reserve took the unusual step of agreeing to backstop up to $30 billion in troubled Bear Stearns assets, invoking emergency lending authority under Section 13(3) of the Federal Reserve Act — rarely used since the Great Depression.

**Aftermath:** The deal closed in June 2008. The rapid collapse of Bear Stearns raised alarms about counterparty risk, leverage, and the fragility of investment banks reliant on overnight funding — issues that would resurface just six months later with the failure of Lehman Brothers, deepening the global financial crisis.

*This account reflects publicly reported events; for detailed reporting, consult primary financial news archives from March 2008.*

# The Fed's Emergency Intervention: How the Federal Reserve Facilitated JPMorgan's Purchase of Bear Stearns

## Introduction

In March 2008, the American financial system faced one of its first major tremors of what would become the Global Financial Crisis. The near-collapse of Bear Stearns, once the fifth-largest investment bank in the United States, forced the Federal Reserve into an unprecedented intervention that would reshape the landscape of American finance and set a template for crisis management that would be repeated throughout 2008.

## The Collapse of Bear Stearns

Bear Stearns had been a Wall Street institution for 85 years, but by early 2008, it was drowning in exposure to mortgage-backed securities and subprime debt. As housing prices continued their decline and confidence in mortgage-related assets evaporated, Bear Stearns found itself increasingly unable to meet its short-term financing obligations.

The crisis reached a fever pitch in the second week of March 2008. Rumors about Bear Stearns' liquidity problems spread rapidly through financial markets, triggering what amounted to a classic bank run—except this run occurred among institutional counterparties and repo market lenders rather than retail depositors lining up outside branches.

By Thursday, March 13, Bear Stearns' cash reserves had plummeted alarmingly. The firm's CEO, Alan Schwartz, contacted the Federal Reserve Bank of New York to inform officials that Bear Stearns would likely need to file for bankruptcy the following morning unless emergency funding could be secured.

## The Federal Reserve's Emergency Response

### Initial Emergency Funding

Recognizing the systemic risk that a disorderly Bear Stearns bankruptcy could pose—given its extensive interconnections with other financial institutions through derivatives contracts, repo agreements, and counterparty relationships—the Federal Reserve moved with unusual speed.

On March 14, 2008, the Federal Reserve Bank of New York, in coordination with JPMorgan Chase, arranged emergency funding for Bear Stearns. This arrangement was structured so that JPMorgan would borrow money from the Fed's discount window and then relend it to Bear Stearns, since Bear Stearns itself, as an investment bank rather than a commercial bank, did not have direct access to the Fed's discount window facilities at that time.

This arrangement provided only temporary relief. It became clear over that weekend that Bear Stearns needed a more permanent solution—specifically, acquisition by a stronger institution—to avoid a disorderly collapse.

### The Weekend Negotiations

What followed was an extraordinary weekend of negotiations, March 14-16, 2008, involving the Federal Reserve, the Treasury Department, JPMorgan Chase, and Bear Stearns executives. Federal Reserve Chairman Ben Bernanke, along with New York Fed President Timothy Geithner, worked feverishly to broker a deal that would prevent Bear Stearns from filing for bankruptcy on Monday morning.

JPMorgan Chase CEO Jamie Dimon emerged as the logical acquirer, given his firm's relative strength and its existing clearing relationship with Bear Stearns. However, JPMorgan was reluctant to absorb the full extent of Bear Stearns' toxic mortgage-related assets without some form of government support.

### The Fed's Unprecedented Financial Backstop

To facilitate the deal, the Federal Reserve took an extraordinary step: it agreed to provide $30 billion in financing to support the acquisition, specifically to backstop Bear Stearns' most troubled and illiquid assets, primarily mortgage-related securities. This arrangement was structured through a special purpose vehicle that would hold these assets, with the Fed providing a non-recourse loan.

This intervention was significant because it marked the first time since the Great Depression that the Federal Reserve invoked its emergency lending authority under Section 13(3) of the Federal Reserve Act to provide direct assistance to a non-bank financial institution outside its traditional regulatory purview. This use of emergency powers signaled how seriously the Fed viewed the systemic risks at stake.

### Terms of the Deal

The initial deal, announced on Sunday, March 16, 2008, valued Bear Stearns at just $2 per share—a stunning collapse for a company that had traded above $150 per share just a year earlier. This price reflected not just Bear Stearns' financial distress but also served as a deliberate signal that the Fed and JPMorgan wanted to avoid the appearance of rewarding failed risk management with an attractive acquisition price.

The extraordinarily low price sparked immediate controversy and legal concerns among Bear Stearns shareholders. Some Bear Stearns employees, who held significant portions of their compensation in company stock, faced devastating losses. Amid shareholder backlash and legal threats, JPMorgan later renegotiated the price upward to approximately $10 per share—still a fraction of the company's prior value, but reflecting concerns about shareholder lawsuits and employee retention.

## Reactions from Treasury Secretary Paulson

Treasury Secretary Henry Paulson, who had come to the role after a career at Goldman Sachs, played a crucial supporting role in the Bear Stearns intervention, though the Federal Reserve took the lead given its regulatory and lending authorities.

Paulson publicly supported the Fed's actions, framing the intervention as necessary to prevent broader financial contagion. In statements following the deal's announcement, Paulson emphasized that the government's goal was to promote market stability and protect the broader financial system, not to bail out Bear Stearns' shareholders or management, who he noted would face substantial losses under the deal's terms.

Paulson was careful to draw a distinction between protecting the financial system and rescuing individual firms or their stakeholders. He stated that the low acquisition price and the wipeout of most shareholder value demonstrated that this was not a bailout in the traditional sense, but rather a market-based solution facilitated by temporary government support.

However, Paulson also acknowledged the extraordinary nature of the intervention. He recognized that the Fed's actions represented a significant departure from traditional central bank operations and indicated that regulatory reforms would likely be necessary to address the risks posed by large, interconnected financial institutions operating outside the traditional banking regulatory framework.

Paulson worked closely with Bernanke throughout the weekend negotiations, and Treasury officials were deeply involved in discussions about the appropriate government response, even though the Fed's balance sheet and legal authorities were the primary tools deployed.

## White House Reaction

The Bush administration, watching the unfolding crisis from the White House, offered public support for the Fed's intervention while attempting to project confidence in the broader stability of the financial system.

White House Press Secretary Dana Perino addressed the Bear Stearns situation in press briefings following the deal's announcement, emphasizing that President Bush had been kept informed of developments throughout the weekend crisis negotiations. The administration characterized the Fed's actions as appropriate and necessary steps to maintain market stability.

President Bush himself, when addressing the matter publicly, sought to reassure Americans about the fundamental soundness of the U.S. financial system while acknowledging the challenges posed by the housing market downturn. The administration's messaging attempted to balance two objectives: supporting the emergency intervention as necessary and prudent, while avoiding language that might suggest panic or a systemic crisis that could further unnerve markets.

Administration officials, including Paulson himself in his dual role representing both Treasury and, informally, the administration's broader economic policy stance, emphasized that the actions taken were consistent with the administration's general philosophy of allowing markets to function while providing targeted intervention only when systemic stability was genuinely at risk.

The White House also faced questions about moral hazard—concerns that bailing out large financial institutions might encourage excessive risk-taking in the future, since firms might assume the government would intervene to prevent their failure. Administration officials pushed back against characterizing the Bear Stearns deal as a "bailout," pointing to the near-total loss suffered by Bear Stearns shareholders and the fact that no Bear Stearns executives received a windfall from the transaction.

## Market and Political Reactions

The deal drew mixed reactions from various quarters. Some market participants and economists praised the swift action for preventing what could have been a catastrophic, disorderly unwinding of Bear Stearns' vast portfolio of derivatives and other financial contracts, which some estimated could have triggered a much broader financial crisis.

Critics, however, raised concerns about the precedent being set. Questions emerged about:

- Whether the Federal Reserve had exceeded its traditional mandate
- Whether taxpayers were being exposed to excessive risk through the $30 billion backstop
- Whether the intervention would encourage reckless behavior by other financial institutions expecting similar treatment
- Whether adequate congressional oversight existed for such emergency actions

Members of Congress from both parties expressed concern about the extent of executive branch and Federal Reserve authority being exercised without direct congressional approval, foreshadowing debates that would intensify later in 2008 as the financial crisis deepened and additional interventions became necessary.

## Long-term Implications

The Bear Stearns rescue established several important precedents:

1. **Expanded Fed Authority**: The use of Section 13(3) emergency lending powers demonstrated that the Federal Reserve was willing to use its full legal authority to address systemic risks, setting a precedent for subsequent interventions.

2. **Too Big to Fail Concerns**: The rescue intensified debates about whether certain financial institutions had become too large and interconnected to be allowed to fail, regardless of their risk management failures.

3. **Regulatory Reform Discussions**: The intervention highlighted gaps in the regulatory framework, particularly regarding investment banks that operated outside traditional banking regulations but posed similar systemic risks.

4. **Template for Future Actions**: The cooperative approach between the Federal Reserve, Treasury, and private sector actors established a model that would be referenced, though not always followed identically, in subsequent interventions throughout the 2008 financial crisis, including the more complex and ultimately different approaches taken with Lehman Brothers, AIG, and other institutions.

## Conclusion

The Federal Reserve's facilitation of JPMorgan's acquisition of Bear Stearns represented a watershed moment in American financial regulatory history. The unprecedented use of emergency lending authority to support a non-bank financial institution's acquisition demonstrated both the Fed's willingness to act decisively during crisis conditions and the significant risks inherent in the modern, interconnected financial system.

The reactions from Treasury Secretary Paulson and the White House reflected an attempt to balance necessary intervention with concerns about moral hazard and government overreach into private markets—tensions that would continue to define policy responses throughout the deepening financial crisis of 2008. While the immediate crisis was averted, the episode raised fundamental questions about financial regulation, systemic risk, and the appropriate role of government intervention in private markets that would occupy policymakers for years to come, ultimately contributing to comprehensive financial reform legislation in the form of the Dodd-Frank Act passed in 2010.

The Bear Stearns episode, in retrospect, served as a preview of the much larger and more complex crisis that would engulf the financial system just six months later with the collapse of Lehman Brothers—a crisis that would test whether the lessons learned from the Bear Stearns intervention could be successfully applied to an even more severe systemic threat.

# JPMorgan buys Bear Stearns for $2 a share

**Fed-backed rescue aims to head off Wall Street crisis**

NEW YORK (CNNMoney.com) -- JPMorgan Chase said Sunday it will acquire Bear Stearns for a mere $2 a share in a stock swap, a fire-sale price that reflects just how close the storied investment bank came to collapse after a weekend scramble to save it.

The deal, brokered with unusual urgency by the Federal Reserve and the Treasury Department, values Bear Stearns at roughly $236 million — a stunning fall for a firm that was trading above $170 a share as recently as last year and closed Friday at $30.

The Federal Reserve took the extraordinary step of agreeing to fund up to $30 billion of Bear Stearns' less liquid assets, a move designed to give JPMorgan the confidence to move forward with the deal and to prevent a disorderly collapse that officials feared could ripple through the broader financial system.

"This is a Fed that is trying to prevent systemic risk to the financial system," said one senior official familiar with the negotiations. "Bear Stearns' failure could have potentially resulted in a chaotic unwinding of positions across the markets."

## A weekend of frantic talks

The agreement came together after a weekend of emergency meetings among Bear Stearns executives, JPMorgan officials, and regulators, following a run on the bank that saw its liquidity evaporate in a matter of days. Clients and lenders, spooked by mounting concerns over Bear's exposure to mortgage-related securities, pulled back so quickly that the firm's cash reserves nearly ran dry by midweek.

"We were subject to a state of panic in the market," Bear Stearns CEO Alan Schwartz said in a statement. "Clearly, the price reflects the value of a company that was under tremendous pressure."

JPMorgan Chase CEO Jamie Dimon struck a measured tone, framing the acquisition as both an opportunity and a rescue.

"Bear Stearns' brand, particularly in trading and capital markets and its prime brokerage business, is testament to the quality of the franchise," Dimon said. "This is a fair deal for all sides given the current environment."

## Market and political reaction

The news is likely to dominate trading when markets open Monday, with analysts warning of continued volatility across financial stocks. Investors have grown increasingly anxious in recent months over the health of major Wall Street firms amid the widening credit crisis, and Bear Stearns' near-collapse has intensified fears that other institutions could face similar liquidity crunches.

Treasury Secretary Henry Paulson defended the government's involvement, saying officials had acted to protect the broader economy rather than to bail out a single firm's shareholders.

"We've been monitoring developments in financial markets very closely," Paulson said. "The government's actions today were focused on facilitating a fair and orderly outcome, not on protecting the shareholders or management of any individual institution."

Federal Reserve Chairman Ben Bernanke echoed that sentiment, emphasizing that the central bank's financing arrangement was necessary to preserve stability.

"The Federal Reserve board voted unanimously to approve this transaction, which will bolster market liquidity and help promote orderly market functioning," Bernanke said. "The Federal Reserve will continue to provide liquidity as necessary to promote the orderly functioning of the financial system."

## What's next

The deal still requires shareholder approval, and some analysts questioned whether Bear Stearns investors — many of whom are company employees holding a significant stake in the firm — would accept a price so far below the stock's recent trading levels. Others noted that with the firm on the brink of bankruptcy, shareholders may have little choice but to approve the transaction.

JPMorgan said it expects the deal to close by the end of the second quarter, pending regulatory and shareholder approval. The combined firm will create one of the largest players in investment banking, though questions remain about job losses, the fate of Bear Stearns' Madison Avenue headquarters, and how markets will digest the speed and scale of the government's intervention.

For now, Wall Street is bracing for a turbulent open.

*—CNNMoney.com staff*
